title: Reproduction Picture Quiz
release_status: Expanded lecture practice with image-based explanations.

questions.stem: Why does the average boy end up taller than the average girl, based on the growth curves?
options: Girls peak earlier, but boys peak later with a larger velocity over a longer growth period
Both sexes reach peak height velocity at the same age with the same peak size
Boys reach peak height velocity earlier than girls but sustain growth for a shorter time
Girls peak later and have a larger peak velocity, so girls end up the taller sex
questions.explanation: Step 1. On the height velocity curves, the female peak (around age 12) occurs earlier than the male peak (around age 14). Step 2. The male peak comes later in pubertal development, is larger than the female peak, and both factors account for the adult height difference between the sexes.
choice_rationales: The male spurt is later and larger, so boys end up taller.
The curves peak at different ages.
The male peak comes after, not before, the female peak.
The male peak is later and larger, not the female.

questions.case_context: A 12-year-old girl and her 12-year-old male classmate are both 10th percentile for height. Their pediatrician tells them the girl will likely grow faster this year and the boy will not reach his fastest growth for about two more years.

questions.stem: Which pair of events is expected first in each sex, and what is the later order?
options: Girls start with breast budding, then pubic hair, growth spurt and menses, while boys start with testicular growth, then penile enlargement, pubic hair and a later growth spurt
Girls start with menarche, then breast budding and pubic hair, while boys start with voice deepening followed by growth spurts in both sexes
Girls start with pubic hair and a growth spurt before breast budding, while boys start with penile enlargement followed by testicular growth and pubic hair
Both sexes start with the growth spurt, then breast budding in girls and testicular growth in boys, followed by pubic hair and menarche in girls
questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture states that in girls the first change is breast budding, often followed by pubic hair, then the growth spurt, then the period. Step 2. In boys the first change is testicular enlargement and growth of the scrotum, followed by voice deepening, penile enlargement, and pubic hair, with the growth spurt in boys happening later than in girls. Events overlap in real life, but exam questions usually follow this order.
choice_rationales: Breast budding and testicular and scrotal growth start puberty in each sex, followed by the later events listed.
Menarche and voice deepening come after earlier changes, not first.
Pubic hair and penile enlargement follow breast budding and testicular growth.
The growth spurt is not first, and in boys it comes later.

questions.stem: Why is the nuclear location of the stain expected, and how will it affect therapy?
options: ER alpha is a nuclear receptor, and ER positive tumors benefit from endocrine therapy such as tamoxifen
ER alpha is a cytoplasmic enzyme, and ER positive tumors predict benefit from conventional chemotherapy alone
ER alpha is a secreted growth factor protein, and ER positive tumors predict no benefit from any hormonal therapy
ER alpha is a membrane receptor, and ER positive tumors predict benefit from the anti HER2 antibody trastuzumab
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nuclear brown staining is the pattern of estrogen receptor alpha, which is almost always expressed in the nucleus of ER positive cells. Step 2. Breast tumors are routinely tested for ER, PR, and HER2, and ER positive tumors predict beneficial responses to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), whereas trastuzumab applies to HER2 positive tumors.
choice_rationales: ER alpha is nuclear and predicts response to endocrine therapy.
ER is a nuclear receptor and not a cytoplasmic enzyme.
ER positivity predicts a benefit from endocrine therapy.
Trastuzumab targets HER2, not ER.

questions.stem: Which test would most readily confirm the cause of her infection?
options: Tzanck preparation of a vesicle scraping
KOH preparation or fungal culture of vulvar and vaginal swabs
Whiff test with potassium hydroxide to detect amines
Wet mount looking for rapidly moving flagellated organisms
questions.explanation: Step 1. The smear shows branching pseudohyphae crossing squamous cells, so she has vulvovaginal candidiasis. Step 2. Candidiasis is usually confirmed by a KOH preparation or fungal culture, and the vulva as well as the vagina should be swabbed. A species-identifying culture helps in recurrent disease.
choice_rationales: A Tzanck preparation looks for herpetic multinucleated cells from a vesicle. She has no vesicles or ulcers.
KOH preparation or fungal culture is the usual confirmatory test for Candida, and swabbing the vulva as well as the vagina improves yield.
A positive whiff test is used for bacterial vaginosis, where anaerobes release amines. This patient has a curdlike discharge and fungal forms, not a fishy odor.
Rapid motility and flagella identify Trichomonas on a wet mount, which causes a purulent yellow-green discharge rather than a curdlike one.

visual_clues: Long filamentous fungal forms cross and entangle the squamous cells.
Their shape and length differ from a fine bacterial coating.
questions.visual_target: Which organism form crosses the squamous cells in this smear?
questions.ground_truth_confidence: high for the stated visual target
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible morphology checked against supplied lecture page and extraction provenance.
questions.case_context: A 29-year-old woman has intense vulvar itching, dysuria, and a thick white curdlike vaginal discharge. Her Pap smear is shown.
questions.condition_overview: Candida vulvovaginitis is a yeast infection, most often from Candida albicans, that overgrows when the vaginal flora or immune balance shifts, for example after antibiotics, with diabetes, pregnancy, or immunosuppression. Patients have itching, burning, and a thick white curd-like discharge. On a Pap smear or tissue section the fungus appears as pale budding yeast and long, branching pseudohyphae that thread through and between squamous cells (the shish kebab appearance), often with neutrophils. It is a superficial infection of keratin and mucosa and does not invade deeply in healthy hosts. Treatment is with topical or oral azole antifungals.

questions.stem: Which outcome is the most important concern for her management at this gestational age?
options: Progression to invasive vulvar squamous cell carcinoma
Tubal scarring that will cause infertility
Preterm labor from ascending protozoal infection
Life-threatening neonatal infection acquired at delivery
questions.explanation: Step 1. Multinucleated cells with nuclear molding indicate herpes simplex infection. Step 2. Neonatal herpes can be life-threatening, so recognizing genital herpes in a woman near term is particularly important. Preterm labor is linked to trichomoniasis, and infertility is a consequence of gonorrhea and chlamydia.
choice_rationales: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is linked to high-risk HPV or lichen sclerosus and does not follow herpes simplex infection.
Infertility from tubal damage is associated with Neisseria and Chlamydia infection, not with herpes.
Preterm labor is associated with Trichomonas infection and the organisms Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma hominis, not with herpes.
Herpes in a pregnant woman near term can cause life-threatening neonatal disease, which makes timely diagnosis important.

questions.case_context: A 28-year-old woman at 38 weeks of gestation has painful vulvar vesicles and ulcers that began 5 days after a new sexual contact. She also has fever, malaise, and tender inguinal lymph nodes. A cervical smear shows the large cells below.
questions.condition_overview: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection of the genital tract causes painful grouped vesicles that rupture into shallow ulcers. The virus infects squamous epithelial cells and produces a distinctive cytopathic effect. Infected cells become enlarged and multinucleated, with nuclei that mold against each other, ground-glass chromatin, and eosinophilic intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions surrounded by a thin rim of marginated chromatin. Biopsy of a blister edge shows epidermal necrosis and acantholysis with inflammation. The virus then lies latent in sensory ganglia and reactivates. Treatment is with acyclovir-type antivirals.

questions.stem: Which long-term risk should she be counseled about?
options: A slightly increased chance of squamous cell carcinoma
Malignant transformation to a papillary hidradenoma of the vulva
Development of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) of the vagina
Obligate progression to differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
questions.explanation: Step 1. Thin epithelium over a band of pale superficial dermal sclerosis with a deep lymphocytic band is lichen sclerosus. Step 2. It is not premalignant but carries a slightly increased chance of squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent or changing lesions should be rebiopsied.
choice_rationales: Lichen sclerosus is not premalignant but confers a slightly increased chance of squamous cell carcinoma.
Papillary hidradenoma is a benign apocrine tumor and is not a malignant transformation of lichen sclerosus.
Sarcoma botryoides is a rare vaginal tumor of young children and is not related to lichen sclerosus.
Lichen sclerosus is not an obligate precursor. The lecture states it is not premalignant.
questions.tested_concept: Which long-term risk should she be counseled about?
visual_clues: The epidermis is relatively thin over a broad pale superficial dermal band.
A deeper inflammatory zone contrasts with the pale sclerotic band.

questions.ground_truth_confidence: high for the stated visual target
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible morphology checked against supplied lecture page and extraction provenance.
questions.case_context: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has severe vulvar itching and dyspareunia. Examination shows white, thinned patches with narrowing of the introitus. A biopsy is shown.
questions.condition_overview: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, probably autoimmune inflammatory skin disorder that mainly affects the vulva and perianal skin of postmenopausal women and also the penis (balanitis xerotica obliterans). Patients have intense itching and white, thin, parchment-like plaques that cause architectural change such as loss of labia minora and a narrowed introitus. Microscopically the epidermis is thin with loss of rete ridges, the superficial dermis is pale and homogenized (sclerotic), and a band of lymphocytes lies beneath it. It carries a small increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent or ulcerated areas are biopsied. First-line therapy is a potent topical corticosteroid.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how this lesion differs from endometriosis?
options: The lesion is composed of smooth muscle cells rather than endometrial-type tissue
The glands and stroma lie on the peritoneal surface rather than within the uterine wall
The lesion is a precursor of serous carcinoma rather than a benign ectopic focus
The glands and stroma lie within the myometrium rather than outside the uterus
questions.explanation: Step 1. Endometrial glands and stroma lie among the smooth muscle bundles, so this is adenomyosis. Step 2. Adenomyosis places endometrial tissue deep in the myometrium, well beyond the normal endometrial interface, while endometriosis places endometrial-type glands and stroma in an extrauterine site. This difference explains why the uterus itself enlarges.
choice_rationales: Smooth muscle proliferation without endometrial glands describes a leiomyoma, which is a discrete whorled nodule rather than glands embedded in muscle.
Peritoneal implants describe superficial endometriosis, not a lesion embedded in the uterine wall.
Serous carcinoma precursors arise in the tube or endometrium and look atypical and crowded, whereas these glands are benign endometrial-type tissue.
Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma inside the myometrium, which is why the uterine wall thickens, while endometriosis is extrauterine.
questions.tested_concept: Adenomyosis versus endometriosis by location of ectopic endometrium
visual_clues: Endometrial-type glands and densely cellular stroma lie within smooth muscle.
The supplied uterine location distinguishes this task from an extrauterine endometriosis specimen.

questions.case_context: A 46-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and a diffusely enlarged, globular uterus. A hysterectomy specimen is sectioned and a representative microscopic field from the wall is shown.

feedback_focus.label: Endometrial gland with adjacent darker stroma within smooth muscle.

questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains her bleeding?
options: Direct invasion of the cervix by an ovarian germ cell tumor
Tumor secretion of estrogen causing prolonged endometrial stimulation
Production of alpha-fetoprotein causing endometrial breakdown
Obstruction of the endometrial cavity by a mature cystic teratoma
questions.explanation: Step 1. Rosette-like follicle-like arrangements point to a granulosa cell tumor, a feminizing sex cord stromal tumor. Step 2. Estrogen from the tumor causes persistent proliferative stimulation of the endometrium, a recognized route to hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma, so postmenopausal bleeding should prompt endometrial evaluation.
choice_rationales: Germ cell tumors do not typically bleed by cervical invasion, and this pattern is not a germ cell tumor.
Granulosa cell tumors are feminizing, and prolonged unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium explains the bleeding and the thickened lining.
Alpha-fetoprotein is made by yolk sac tumors, which occur in younger patients, and does not drive endometrial bleeding.
A mature cystic teratoma is a cystic mass with hair and skin structures and does not stimulate the endometrium.
questions.tested_concept: Estrogen-producing granulosa cell tumor causing endometrial pathology
visual_clues: Small groups of tumor cells surround rounded pink material.
These small rosettelike formations are the target rather than the whole tumor architecture.
questions.visual_target: Which named structure is visible in this ovarian tumor field?
questions.ground_truth_confidence: high for the stated visual target
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible morphology checked against supplied lecture page and extraction provenance.
questions.case_context: A 52-year-old woman has postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a solid ovarian mass and thickened endometrium. The ovarian mass is sampled and shows small rosette-like groups of cells around pink material.
questions.condition_overview: Granulosa cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary that often secretes estrogen, causing precocious puberty in girls, or abnormal bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma in older women. Microscopically small uniform cells with pale grooved (coffee-bean) nuclei form microfollicular patterns around Call-Exner bodies (small spaces with eosinophilic material), and tumor cells stain for inhibin and calretinin. Most are low grade and unilateral, but late recurrence can occur. Treatment is surgery.

questions.stem: What is the most likely origin of the ovarian tumor?
options: Metastasis from a mucin producing carcinoma such as the stomach
A granulosa cell tumor that secretes estrogen and causes endometrial hyperplasia
A germ cell tumor arising from primitive embryonal cells of the ovary
A primary ovarian serous carcinoma arising from tubal type epithelium
questions.explanation: Step 1. Signet-ring cells indicate a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma. Step 2. In a patient with prior gastric cancer and bilateral solid ovarian masses, this is a metastasis to the ovary, a Krukenberg tumor, rather than a primary ovarian tumor.
choice_rationales: Signet-ring mucin-filled cells with a gastric history and bilateral masses indicate metastasis, which is the Krukenberg pattern.
Granulosa cell tumors show follicle-like rosettes and oval grooved nuclei, not intracellular mucin.
Germ cell tumors show primitive cells, Schiller-Duval bodies, or sheets of large pale cells, not signet-ring cells.
Primary serous carcinoma is papillary with psammoma bodies and slitlike spaces, not signet-ring cells.
questions.tested_concept: What is the most likely origin of the ovarian tumor?

questions.case_context: A 44-year-old woman has bilateral solid ovarian masses discovered during evaluation. Her history includes a prior gastric resection for cancer. Microscopy of an ovarian mass shows cells with large mucin vacuoles pushing the nuclei aside.
questions.condition_overview: Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis to the ovary, usually bilateral, from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often of the stomach, and also the colon or breast. The ovaries are enlarged and nodular. Microscopically, signet-ring cells with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus infiltrate a cellular, reactive ovarian stroma, often with mucin pools. Prognosis is poor and depends on the primary site, and the finding of a bilateral solid ovarian mass should prompt a search for a gastrointestinal primary.

questions.stem: Which tumor is most consistent with her clinical picture?
options: Mature cystic teratoma
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
Yolk sac tumor
Granulosa cell tumor
questions.explanation: Step 1. Bright rodlike cytoplasmic crystals mark Leydig-type cells. Step 2. Sertoli and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors are the virilizing sex cord stromal tumors, which explains hirsutism and voice deepening, whereas granulosa cell tumors are feminizing.
choice_rationales: A mature cystic teratoma contains hair, teeth, and skin structures and is not a virilizing tumor.
Sertoli-Leydig tumors are virilizing and contain Leydig-type cells, matching the androgen excess.
Yolk sac tumors secrete alpha-fetoprotein and are not hormone producing in this way.
Granulosa cell tumors are feminizing and produce estrogen effects, not virilization.

visual_clues: Bright red angular rods lie inside the cells.

questions.stem: Which serum marker would be expected to be elevated?
options: Beta-hCG as the dominant marker
Calcitonin
Alpha-fetoprotein
CA-125 as a specific marker of the germ cell component
questions.explanation: Step 1. A papillation with a central blood vessel is a Schiller-Duval body, diagnostic of yolk sac tumor, a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor of extraembryonic differentiation. Step 2. Yolk sac tumors produce alpha-fetoprotein, seen as hyaline PAS positive bodies and AFP immunoreactivity, so serum AFP is the expected marker.
choice_rationales: Beta-hCG is associated with trophoblastic differentiation such as choriocarcinoma, which is not shown here.
Calcitonin is a thyroid C cell product and has no role in this tumor.
Alpha-fetoprotein is made by yolk sac tumor and is the expected marker.
CA-125 is not described in the lecture as the marker of a germ cell tumor.

questions.condition_overview: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. Microscopically a loose reticular or lacelike pattern of cuboidal cells surrounds open spaces. Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space, and eosinophilic hyaline globules are common. Tumor cells secrete alpha-fetoprotein, which is a serum marker. It is chemosensitive.

questions.stem: What is the fate of these follicles, and how does it differ from the follicle that ovulates?
options: They degenerated by atresia and never ovulated, unlike the dominant follicle that ruptures
They are mature Graafian follicles that are about to release an oocyte at midcycle
They are luteinized granulosa cell sheets that are making progesterone after ovulation
They ovulated already and are turning into corpora albicantia over 10 to 14 days
questions.explanation: Step 1. Irregular follicles with a glassy membrane and degenerated oocyte and granulosa cells are atretic follicles. Step 2. Most follicles are lost this way (about 1 million oocytes at birth fall to about 400,000 at puberty), whereas only the dominant follicle ruptures and becomes a corpus luteum.
choice_rationales: Atresia is degeneration of oocyte and granulosa cells, and only the dominant follicle ovulates.
A Graafian follicle has a large fluid-filled antrum and intact granulosa, not a collapsed outline.
Large pale luteinized granulosa cells characterize the corpus luteum, not atretic follicles.
A corpus albicans is the scar of a degenerated corpus luteum and is not a collapsed follicle with a glassy membrane.
questions.tested_concept: What is the fate of these follicles, and how does it differ from the follicle that ovulates?

questions.stem: Which pattern could explain her constant leakage, and what is the developmental basis?
options: Complete duplication as in D, because a second ureteric bud descends with the mesonephric duct and can open low in the urethra or vagina
Complete duplication as in D, because the ureteric bud failed to branch and no collecting ducts formed in the lower pole
Partial duplication as in E, because the two ureters fuse before the bladder and enter at the normal trigone, causing no leakage
Complete duplication as in D, because the upper pole ureter inserts above the lower pole ureter and both open normally at the trigone
questions.explanation: Step 1. Duplication of the ureter comes from early splitting of the ureteric bud, and the split may be partial (ureters join, as in E) or complete (separate ureters, as in D). Step 2. In some complete duplications one bud keeps a normal position while the abnormal bud moves down with the mesonephric duct and has a low entrance into the urethra, vagina, or vestibule. An opening below the bladder fits constant dribbling alongside normal voiding, which is an inference from the lecture site list. A partial duplication ends in one distal segment, so it does not create a second low opening.
choice_rationales: The lecture says the abnormal bud descends with the mesonephric duct and opens in the urethra, vagina, or vestibule.
Failure of the bud to branch causes dysplasia or agenesis, not a duplicated system.
A partial duplication has one distal segment, so it has no second abnormal opening to leak urine.
Constant leakage requires an ectopic opening of the abnormal ureter low in the urethra or vagina, not two normal trigone openings.

questions.case_context: A 4-year-old girl dribbles urine all day even though she also voids normally. An ultrasound shows a duplicated collecting system on one side. The teaching specimens compared in panels D and E show two patterns of ureteral duplication. In D the two ureters stay separate all the way to the bladder, and in E they join into a single distal segment.
questions.condition_overview: Ureteral duplication results from early or double branching of the ureteric bud. Partial duplication has two ureters that join before the bladder, and complete duplication has two separate ureters with separate bladder openings. In complete duplication the upper-pole ureter inserts lower and medially (Weigert-Meyer rule) and tends to be obstructed, while the lower-pole ureter inserts higher and tends to reflux. It predisposes to infection and hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: Which developmental event best explains both the fusion and the low position?
options: The lower poles fused while the kidneys passed the umbilical artery fork, and the inferior mesenteric artery then blocked ascent
Accessory renal arteries persisted and tethered the lower poles of both kidneys to the pelvis during ascent
Both kidneys failed to ascend because short ureters held the lower poles together at the pelvic brim
The ureteric bud failed to contact the metanephric mesoderm on one side, so one kidney never formed and the other crossed the midline
questions.explanation: Step 1. A band of renal tissue joining the lower poles is a horseshoe kidney. Step 2. The lecture explains that during ascent the kidneys pass through the arterial fork formed by the umbilical arteries and can be pushed so close that the lower poles fuse. The isthmus then catches on the root of the inferior mesenteric artery, which prevents ascent, so the kidney sits low, and the ureters pass ventral to the isthmus. It occurs in about 1 in 600 people.
choice_rationales: Lower pole fusion in the arterial fork plus arrest under the inferior mesenteric artery explains fusion and low position.
Accessory arteries are a common finding from embryonic vessels but do not fuse or lower the kidneys.
Short ureters do not fuse the kidneys, because fusion arises when the lower poles meet in the arterial fork and the inferior mesenteric artery arrests ascent.
Failed bud and mesoderm contact produces agenesis or hypoplasia, whereas a fused pair with an isthmus below the inferior mesenteric artery is a horseshoe kidney.
questions.tested_concept: Which developmental event best explains both the fusion and the low position?

questions.case_context: A 31-year-old man has a CT for abdominal pain. The study shows the two kidneys joined across the midline by a broad band of renal tissue in front of the aorta. Both lie lower than usual, at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae.
questions.condition_overview: Horseshoe kidney is a congenital fusion of the lower poles of the two kidneys across the midline by an isthmus, usually located low in the abdomen because the isthmus is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent. It is the most common renal fusion anomaly and is associated with Turner syndrome. Most patients are asymptomatic, but ureteropelvic obstruction, infection, and stones are more common.

questions.stem: At which level of the HPG axis is her defect, and which of the listed diagnoses best explains it?
options: Hypothalamic level, due to functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from an eating disorder
Gonadal level, due to Turner syndrome with streak ovaries and elevated FSH
Outflow tract level, due to an imperforate hymen with obstructed menstrual flow
Pituitary level, due to a prolactinoma suppressing gonadotropin release
questions.explanation: Step 1. Low LH, low FSH, and low estradiol with weight loss show suppression of the axis at the hypothalamus (decreased GnRH pulsation). Step 2. Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is caused by eating disorders, chronic disease, celiac disease, and relative energy deficiency in sport, and this patient's weight loss and normal labs make an eating disorder the cause.
choice_rationales: Low gonadotropins indicate a central defect from energy deficiency.
Turner syndrome would give high FSH and LH, not low.
An outflow obstruction would have normal gonadotropins and estradiol.
Prolactin is normal, so a prolactinoma is not the cause.

questions.case_context: A 15-year-old girl has lost 30 lb over 6 months and has never had a period. Breasts are Tanner stage 4 and pubic hair is Tanner stage 5. Estradiol is below 10, LH is 0.1, FSH is 3.0, and prolactin, TSH, and celiac screen are normal.
questions.condition_overview: In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (central or secondary), the hypothalamus or pituitary fails to produce adequate GnRH, LH, or FSH, so the gonads are underdriven and sex steroids are low. Causes include Kallmann syndrome (with anosmia), pituitary tumors, hyperprolactinemia, functional causes such as low energy availability, and chronic illness. It presents with delayed or absent puberty or amenorrhea, with low LH and FSH, and treatment is directed at the cause, with hormone replacement or gonadotropin therapy for fertility.

questions.stem: Where is the defect in the HPG axis, and which test should be sent?
options: Gonadal level (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), and a karyotype for Turner syndrome
Hypothalamic level, and an MRI of the brain to look for a hypothalamic lesion
Outflow tract level, and a pelvic MRI to look for a uterus and vaginal obstruction
Pituitary level, and a prolactin level to look for a pituitary adenoma
questions.explanation: Step 1. High LH and FSH with low estradiol mean the gonads are not responding, so the lesion is at the gonadal level (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Step 2. Short stature or a webbed neck suggests Turner syndrome, so a karyotype is indicated, and most women with gonadal insufficiency are infertile with permanent absence of puberty.
choice_rationales: Elevated gonadotropins with low estradiol place the defect in the gonad, and karyotype tests for Turner.
A central defect would give low gonadotropins.
An outflow lesion would have normal hormones and normal breast development.
Prolactin does not explain high gonadotropins.

questions.case_context: A 16-year-old girl has no breast development and has never had a period. Height is short, she has a webbed neck, and her estradiol is low. LH and FSH are markedly elevated.
questions.condition_overview: In hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary), the gonads fail despite adequate pituitary drive, so loss of negative feedback from estradiol, testosterone, and inhibin raises FSH and LH. Causes include Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, premature ovarian insufficiency, gonadal injury from chemotherapy or radiation, and autoimmune oophoritis. It presents with delayed puberty or amenorrhea, infertility, and low sex steroids, and treatment is sex hormone replacement.

questions.stem: Which pair of findings would be expected on bedside testing?
options: Pseudohyphae on KOH preparation with a curdlike discharge
Vaginal pH above 4.5 and a fishy odor when KOH is added
Rapidly moving flagellated organisms on a wet mount
Vaginal pH below 4.5 with abundant lactobacilli
questions.explanation: Step 1. Bacterial forms densely coating squamous cells indicate bacterial vaginosis. Step 2. Loss of lactobacilli raises the pH above 4.5, and anaerobes release amines that produce a fishy odor on addition of KOH (the whiff test). Clue cells are present, with no lactobacilli or white blood cells.
choice_rationales: Pseudohyphae with a curdlike discharge describe candidiasis.
Bacterial vaginosis raises the vaginal pH above 4.5, and KOH releases amines from anaerobes to give a positive whiff test.
Rapidly moving flagellated organisms describe trichomoniasis, which gives a purulent yellow-green discharge.
A pH below 4.5 with abundant lactobacilli is the normal flora and would not cause her discharge.

questions.condition_overview: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift from lactobacillus-dominant vaginal flora to an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis. It causes a thin gray, fishy-smelling discharge with an elevated vaginal pH but little true inflammation. The characteristic cytology is the clue cell, a squamous cell whose surface and borders are obscured by a stippled coat of coccobacilli, often with few lymphocytes and few neutrophils. It increases the risk of preterm birth and pelvic infection and is treated with metronidazole or clindamycin.

questions.condition_overview: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, exophytic anogenital wart caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (mainly types 6 and 11). It appears as single or multiple raised, rough, cauliflower-like papules. Microscopically there are papillary fronds of acanthotic squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores, with hyperkeratosis and koilocytes (cells with enlarged wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear clearing) in the upper layers. Condylomata are transmitted sexually, are not generally premalignant, and are treated by ablation, topical therapy, or excision. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

Intense pruritus is typical, and treatment involves high-potency topical corticosteroids and breaking the itch-scratch cycle. Biopsy of persistent lesions excludes lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.condition_overview: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan sexually transmitted infection causing frothy yellow-green malodorous discharge, vulvovaginal itching, dysuria, and a strawberry cervix with punctate hemorrhages, with vaginal pH above 4.5. Wet mount shows motile pear-shaped trophozoites with flagella, and the Pap smear can show pear-shaped organisms. Perinuclear halos in squamous cells can mimic it but are a pseudoparasite. Treatment with metronidazole should include partners.

The tumor cells spread laterally within the epidermis beyond the visible lesion
The tumor arises from an underlying deep carcinoma that remains in place
The tumor is a benign apocrine neoplasm that regrows from myoepithelium
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale cells scattered within the epidermis indicate extramammary (vulvar) Paget disease. Step 2. Paget cells spread laterally, so excision can be incomplete and the disease may recur. Unlike Paget disease of the nipple, it is typically an intraepithelial neoplasm not associated with an underlying cancer.
choice_rationales: Paget disease is not driven by HPV 16, which is associated with classic VIN.
Paget cells spread laterally within the epidermis, so margins may be incomplete and recurrence can follow.
Unlike mammary Paget disease, vulvar Paget disease is typically not associated with an underlying cancer.
Papillary hidradenoma, not Paget disease, is the benign apocrine tumor with myoepithelium.

questions.case_context: A 64-year-old woman has chronic vulvar pruritus and pain. A red-pink and white plaque resembling eczema has not responded to topical therapy. A biopsy shows scattered large pale cells in the epidermis. She has had wide local excision, and the disease has recurred.
questions.condition_overview: Extramammary Paget disease is an uncommon intraepidermal adenocarcinoma, most often on the vulva of older women, that presents as a red, scaly or eczematous, itchy plaque. Microscopically large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm and atypical nuclei are scattered singly and in nests among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, sometimes extending into skin appendages. The cells contain intracytoplasmic mucin (mucicarmine and PAS positive) and are CK7 positive, unlike squamous cells. It is usually confined to the epidermis, but some cases are associated with an underlying adnexal or visceral carcinoma, and the invasive form carries a worse prognosis. Treatment is wide excision.

The tissue is an HPV induced lesion that bleeds with sexual contact
The tissue is a leiomyoma that grows with age and bleeds with menses
The tissue is a germ cell tumor that releases hormones cyclically
questions.explanation: Step 1. Endometrial glands with stroma in an extrauterine site indicate endometriosis. Step 2. The ectopic endometrium functions and undergoes cyclic changes, producing hemorrhage and pain, and it can form ovarian endometriomas called chocolate cysts.
choice_rationales: Ectopic endometrium is functioning tissue that undergoes cyclic changes, so it bleeds and causes pain.
HPV infection causes cervical squamous lesions and has no role in endometriosis.
Leiomyomas are smooth muscle tumors and do not contain endometrial glands with stromal cuffs.
A germ cell tumor would show primitive or teratomatous elements and not endometrial glands with stroma.

questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

Low risk human papillomavirus, mainly types 6 and 11 found in condyloma
Herpes simplex virus type 2, which causes genital ulcers and vesicles
Chlamydia trachomatis, which causes cervicitis and pelvic inflammation

HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types that cause condylomata and benign cervical changes, not most invasive cancers.
HSV causes painful vesicles and ulcers and is not the oncogenic cause of cervical squamous carcinoma.
Chlamydia is a cause of cervicitis and is not the oncogenic agent in cervical squamous carcinoma.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cervical cancer and arises from persistently infected high-risk HPV lesions at the transformation zone through HSIL. Nests of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invade the cervical stroma. It presents with postcoital or abnormal bleeding, or may be found by screening. Staging uses tumor size, parametrial, pelvic wall, and nodal spread. Advanced disease can obstruct the ureters and cause hydronephrosis and renal failure, which is a major cause of death. Treatment is surgery for early disease and chemoradiation with brachytherapy for advanced disease.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive urothelial carcinoma grows beyond the urothelial basement membrane into the lamina propria and, in more advanced disease, the muscularis propria (detrusor), perivesical fat, and beyond. Irregular nests and cords of atypical cells infiltrate between smooth muscle bundles with a desmoplastic stroma. Depth of invasion, especially muscle invasion, is the most important prognostic factor. Muscle-invasive disease is treated by radical cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and urine cytology alone cannot determine depth.

It is a low grade papillary tumor with less than 5 percent risk of progression

questions.condition_overview: Schistosoma haematobium is a trematode acquired from freshwater snail habitats in Africa and the Middle East. Adult worms live in the vesical venous plexus, and eggs deposited in the bladder wall provoke granulomatous inflammation, calcification, fibrosis, and hematuria. Eggs are ovoid with a terminal spine. Chronic infection predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Treatment is praziquantel.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis, and what does the failed estrogen and progestin challenge tell you about the site of the problem?
options: Asherman syndrome, because the uterus cannot respond to hormones due to scarring
Hyperprolactinemia, because prolactin suppresses GnRH
Primary ovarian insufficiency, because the ovary failed and FSH is low
Sheehan syndrome, because the pituitary was damaged by postpartum hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Step 1. Irregular filling defects within the contrast column with amenorrhea after curettage are intrauterine adhesions of Asherman syndrome, whose number one cause is iatrogenic intrauterine manipulation such as D&C. Step 2. No withdrawal bleed after estrogen and progestin means the uterus is not intact or cannot respond, so the problem is the uterine outflow tract, not the hypothalamus, pituitary, or ovary.
choice_rationales: No bleeding after estrogen and progestin points to a uterine scarring problem, as in Asherman.
Hyperprolactinemia is excluded by a normal prolactin level.
POI causes high FSH and would bleed after estrogen and progestin if the uterus is normal.
Sheehan syndrome follows postpartum hemorrhage and would give low gonadotropins.

questions.condition_overview: Asherman syndrome is the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) after endometrial injury, usually from curettage, infection, or surgery. Scarring partially or completely obliterates the uterine cavity and causes hypomenorrhea or amenorrhea, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss. Hysterosalpingography shows irregular filling defects, and hysteroscopy shows pale fibrous bands bridging the cavity. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis followed by measures to restore the endometrium.

questions.condition_overview: Candida vulvovaginitis is a yeast infection, most often from Candida albicans, that overgrows when the vaginal flora or immune balance shifts, for example after antibiotics, with diabetes, pregnancy, or immunosuppression. questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. questions.stem: Which diagnosis and cyst origin fit this infant, and what would the lecture predict about the clinical course?
options: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, with cysts from collecting ducts and renal failure in infancy or childhood
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with cysts from all nephron segments and renal failure that usually appears only in adulthood
Multicystic dysplastic kidney, in which nephrons fail to develop and the ureteric bud fails to branch

The lecture links the recessive form (about 1 in 6,000 births) to cysts from collecting ducts, very large kidneys, and renal failure in infancy or childhood. The dominant form arises from all nephron segments and usually spares kidney function until adulthood. Both are ciliopathies from mutations in cilia proteins. Healthy parents and neonatal presentation favor the recessive form.
choice_rationales: Collecting duct cysts, big kidneys, and early renal failure describe the recessive disease.
The dominant form arises from all nephron segments and usually causes failure only in adulthood.
In multicystic dysplasia the bud fails to branch and nephrons fail to form, so large cystic organs are not expected.
Bilateral agenesis leaves no kidney tissue, giving anuria, oligohydramnios, and hypoplastic lungs.
visual_clues: Multiple small rounded spaces are scattered in both pieces.

questions.stem: What would you expect in this fetus compared with the typical male panel?
options: The urethral folds stay separate like the female panel, because DHT drives phallic elongation and fold closure
The folds join early, because the lack of DHT removes the signal that holds them open
The scrotal swellings become the labia majora and the folds fuse, because the tubercle becomes a clitoris
The urethral folds join normally, because testosterone alone completes the closure process
questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture states that circulating testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase to DHT, which acts through the androgen receptor to masculinize the external genitalia. Step 2. Masculinization means rapid elongation of the phallus, which pulls the urethral folds forward to form the urethral groove, and the folds then close over the urethral plate to form the penile urethra by the end of the third month. Without DHT the folds would be expected to stay open as in the female panel, an inference from that mechanism.
choice_rationales: DHT is the active androgen for phallic elongation and fold closure, so its absence leaves folds apart.
No signal holds the folds open, and lacking DHT would delay rather than hasten midline joining.
The folds would not fuse, so the combination of fused folds with female structures does not follow.
Testosterone is converted to DHT before acting on the external genitalia, so testosterone alone is not enough.
visual_clues: The later male panel shows the ventral folds approaching and joining at the midline. The later female panel retains separated folds.

questions.condition_overview: Asherman syndrome is the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) after endometrial injury, usually from curettage, infection, or surgery. Scarring partially or completely obliterates the uterine cavity and causes hypomenorrhea or amenorrhea, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss. Hysterosalpingography shows irregular filling defects, and hysteroscopy shows pale fibrous bands bridging the cavity. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis followed by measures to restore the endometrium.

questions.stem: What is the underlying syndrome, and why does the mass develop?
options: Swyer syndrome, 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis from SRY mutation, whose streak gonads carry about a 25 percent germ cell tumor risk
Complete androgen insensitivity, with a blind vaginal pouch and absent uterus in a 46,XY patient
Müllerian agenesis (MRKH), with a 46,XX karyotype and streak gonads that carry about a 25 percent germ cell tumor risk
Turner syndrome 45,X, with streak gonads, elevated FSH and LH, and absent breast development
questions.explanation: Step 1. A 46,XY patient with female genitalia, a normal uterus and tubes, streak gonads, absent breast development, and high FSH and LH has Swyer syndrome, caused by SRY mutation with no AMH or testosterone and no estrogen. Step 2. Streak gonads need removal because of an increased risk (25 percent) of germ cell tumors, most commonly gonadoblastoma, and a dysgerminoma can occur.
choice_rationales: Swyer syndrome has streak gonads that carry a tumor risk and a normal uterus.
Complete androgen insensitivity has an absent uterus and normal breast development.
MRKH has a 46,XX karyotype with an absent uterus and normal ovarian function, whereas this patient is 46,XY with a normal uterus and streak gonads.
Turner syndrome is 45,X, but this patient is 46,XY with a normal uterus and tubes, which fits Swyer syndrome.
visual_clues: Large round nucleated cells form groups separated by paler stromal tissue with scattered small dark nuclei.
The case slide identifies dysgerminoma. The microscopic task focuses on the grouped architecture.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis, and how does it differ from an imperforate hymen?

Asherman syndrome is an intrauterine adhesion disorder.

The uterus and both tubes remain above the partition.

questions.stem: Which zone of the gland is the usual origin of this process, and why does it cause obstruction?
options: The central zone, which makes up 25 percent of the gland
The seminal vesicle, which wraps the urethra
The peripheral zone, which makes up 70 percent of the gland
The transition zone, whose nodular growth compresses the urethra
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nodules encircling the urethra are benign prostatic hyperplasia (nodular hyperplasia). Step 2. BPH arises mainly in the transition (central) gland around the urethra, so growth compresses the urethral lumen and causes obstruction, whereas cancer typically arises in the peripheral zone and is less likely to obstruct early.
choice_rationales: The central zone is 25 percent of the gland volume but is not the usual BPH origin in the lecture.
The seminal vesicles are separate structures and do not give rise to BPH.
The peripheral zone is the major site of prostatic cancer and lies away from the urethra.
BPH originates in the transition zone around the urethra and compresses it.

questions.case_context: A 72-year-old man has nocturia, weak stream, and incomplete emptying. A transurethral resection specimen from the central gland shows large pale nodules that crowd around the urethral slit.
questions.condition_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a nodular proliferation of glands and stroma in the periurethral transition zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone and increasing with age. Enlarged nodules compress the prostatic urethra, causing hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, and incomplete emptying, with risks of retention, infection, and bladder hypertrophy. Microscopically there are large glands with papillary infoldings with two cell layers, and basal cells are preserved. It does not become cancer. Treatment is with alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, or resection.

questions.stem: Which management is the first-line surgical therapy for patients like him?

Radical orchiectomy
Transurethral resection of the prostate
Orchiopexy
questions.explanation: Step 1. Multiple rounded nodules in an enlarged gland around the urethra indicate benign nodular hyperplasia. Step 2. TURP is first-line surgical therapy for recurrent urinary retention, while alpha blockers reduce muscle tone and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the gland in medical therapy.
choice_rationales: Lymphadenectomy and prostatectomy belong to prostate cancer staging and treatment.
Radical orchiectomy treats testicular germ cell tumors.
TURP is first line for recurrent retention in BPH.
Orchiopexy fixes an undescended testis.

questions.condition_overview: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant tumor of trophoblast with no villi, composed of sheets of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and intermediate trophoblast. It follows a hydatidiform mole, an abortion, or a normal pregnancy, or arises as a germ cell tumor of the testis or ovary. It forms a soft, dark, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass that invades the myometrium and vessels and spreads early to the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. hCG is markedly elevated. It is highly chemosensitive, and vaginal metastases should not be biopsied because they bleed.

It is a seminoma, a homogeneous gray tumor usually confined by the tunica albuginea, with a good prognosis after surgery
It is indolent like a spermatocytic tumor, occurs mostly in older men, and is cured by orchiectomy with no spread
It is always confined by the tunica albuginea and never reaches the cord

Seminoma is usually limited by the tunica albuginea, whereas this fleshy hemorrhagic tumor penetrates it.

questions.condition_overview: Embryonal carcinoma is an aggressive malignant germ cell tumor of the testis and, rarely, the ovary, composed of primitive epithelial cells in glands, papillae, and solid sheets with crowded, overlapping, pleomorphic nuclei and frequent necrosis and hemorrhage. Cells express CD30 and cytokeratin and OCT3/4. The cut surface is variegated with hemorrhagic and necrotic areas. It spreads hematogenously and lymphatically and is a component of many mixed germ cell tumors. Treatment is orchiectomy and chemotherapy.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is supported, and why is it distinct from seminoma?
options: Embryonal carcinoma, since seminoma has large uniform cells with lymphocytes and lacks anaplastic glands
Yolk sac tumor, since CD30 marks it and it forms Schiller-Duval bodies
Choriocarcinoma, since cytokeratin marks it and trophoblastic cells with hemorrhage are seen
Seminoma, since CD30 is its marker and it shows anaplastic cells in solid and glandular patterns
questions.explanation: Step 1. Anaplastic cells in solid and glandular patterns with CD30 and cytokeratin positivity indicate embryonal carcinoma. Step 2. Seminoma shows large round cells with clear cytoplasm in nests divided by fibrous bands with lymphocytes, so the pattern and markers differ.
choice_rationales: Embryonal carcinoma is CD30 and keratin positive with anaplastic cells.
Yolk sac tumor is marked by AFP.
Choriocarcinoma shows trophoblastic cells with hemorrhage, not anaplastic cells in solid and glandular patterns marked by CD30.
Seminoma shows large round clear cells in nests divided by fibrous bands with lymphocytes, and it is marked by OCT3/4 and CD117, not CD30.
visual_clues: Irregular dark nuclei are crowded within solid and poorly organized epithelial groups.
The lecture describes anaplastic cells in testicular embryonal carcinoma.

questions.condition_overview: Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) is the precursor lesion of most testicular germ cell tumors. Large atypical cells with clear cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli line the base of seminiferous tubules next to the basement membrane, and they stain for PLAP, OCT3/4, and CD117. Risk factors include cryptorchidism and gonadal dysgenesis. It can progress to invasive tumors over years.

questions.condition_overview: Leydig cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor of the testis that forms a well-circumscribed, golden-brown, solid nodule. Polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, and sometimes lipofuscin pigment and Reinke crystals form sheets. It secretes androgens or estrogens, causing precocious puberty in boys or gynecomastia in adults. Most are benign and are treated by orchiectomy.

The tumor is a seminal vesicle cyst that does not compress the urethra
The tumor is in the transition zone around the urethra and obstructs urine flow
The tumor is a benign nodular hyperplasia of the central gland that spares the urethra

questions.condition_overview: Prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common nonskin cancer in men and typically arises in the peripheral zone, so it presents late with urinary symptoms and is often found by PSA or digital rectal examination. Small crowded glands infiltrate between benign glands and stroma, lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli, and the basal cell layer is absent (p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin negative), while AMACR is often positive. Grading uses the Gleason system by glandular architecture: pattern 3 well-formed glands, pattern 4 fused or cribriform glands, and pattern 5 solid sheets, cords, or single cells with comedonecrosis. Bone metastases are typically osteoblastic.

questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Cells express OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP. It is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis, and it commonly arises in undescended testes.

questions.condition_overview: Spermatocytic tumor is a rare, benign-behaving testicular tumor of older men, unrelated to germ cell neoplasia in situ. questions.case_context: A 16-year-old boy develops sudden severe testicular pain after sports. The testis is swollen and blue-black. Doppler shows absent flow. He arrives 9 hours after onset.
questions.condition_overview: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that cuts off venous and then arterial blood flow, causing sudden severe scrotal pain, a high-riding testis, and absent cremasteric reflex. It most often affects adolescents with a bell-clapper deformity. Doppler ultrasound shows reduced or absent perfusion on the affected side. Untreated torsion leads to hemorrhagic infarction (dark, swollen testis with coagulative necrosis), and salvage requires surgery within about 6 hours.

questions.stem: What does this histologic finding indicate about the testis?
options: The tissue is nonviable, so the testis was lost to hemorrhagic infarction
The tissue is viable with normal spermatogenesis and preserved interstitial cells
The tissue shows only mild inflammation with preserved tubules and vessels
The tissue is neoplastic, with sheets of atypical germ cells replacing the tubules

questions.condition_overview: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically in women under 35. It is a well-circumscribed, rubbery, freely mobile mass (breast mouse). Phyllodes tumors typically occur around age 50, about 15 years later than fibroadenomas.

questions.condition_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a nodular proliferation of glands and stroma in the periurethral transition zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone and increasing with age. Microscopically there are large glands with papillary infoldings with two cell layers, and basal cells are preserved. It does not become cancer. Treatment is with alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, or resection.

questions.condition_overview: Prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common nonskin cancer in men and typically arises in the peripheral zone, so it presents late with urinary symptoms and is often found by PSA or digital rectal examination. Grading uses the Gleason system by glandular architecture: pattern 3 well-formed glands, pattern 4 fused or cribriform glands, and pattern 5 solid sheets, cords, or single cells with comedonecrosis. Bone metastases are typically osteoblastic.

questions.condition_overview: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma and the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, typically in young women. It forms a solid, pale, fleshy, lobulated mass. Microscopically large round cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. Cells are OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP positive. Tumors are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis. It can occur in gonadal dysgenesis, such as Swyer syndrome.

questions.condition_overview: Candida vulvovaginitis is a yeast infection, most often from Candida albicans, that overgrows when the vaginal flora or immune balance shifts, for example after antibiotics, with diabetes, pregnancy, or immunosuppression. questions.condition_overview: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, probably autoimmune inflammatory skin disorder that mainly affects the vulva and perianal skin of postmenopausal women and also the penis (balanitis xerotica obliterans). questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. questions.stem: What is the most accurate response?

Cysts indicate inflammatory carcinoma and require urgent mastectomy
Cysts are a precursor of ductal carcinoma in situ and need excision to prevent progression
Cysts always carry a 4 to 5 times risk of invasive carcinoma over time, so chemoprevention is indicated
questions.explanation: Step 1. Multiple variably sized cysts represent dilated lobular regions in fibrocystic change. Step 2. Cysts, apocrine change, and adenosis are non-proliferative and do not increase risk, whereas proliferative lesions such as usual hyperplasia or sclerosing adenosis raise risk 1.5 to 2 times.
choice_rationales: Non-proliferative cysts carry no added risk, so the claim of substantially raised risk is wrong unless proliferative change is present.
Inflammatory carcinoma is a clinical entity with skin changes and dermal lymphatic involvement.

questions.condition_overview: Fibrocystic changes are the most common benign breast condition in premenopausal women and cause cyclical pain and lumpiness. Nonproliferative changes carry no added cancer risk, whereas proliferative changes (usual ductal hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis) carry a mild increase, and proliferative disease with atypia a moderate increase.

It is non-proliferative and carries no risk
It mimics invasive carcinoma and mildly increases cancer risk
It represents fat necrosis from trauma
questions.explanation: Step 1. Crowded small glands with sclerotic stroma that keep a lobular outline are sclerosing adenosis. Step 2. It is a proliferative lesion without atypia with a 1.5 to 2 times relative risk and is a cancer mimic with slitlike glands resembling single files.

Invasive ductal carcinoma with a desmoplastic response and infiltrative border
Usual ductal hyperplasia, which carries no increased risk of carcinoma later
Lobular carcinoma in situ, with loosely cohesive cells filling the acini

questions.case_context: A 31-year-old woman has a mass that is stable on ultrasound for two years. Core biopsy shows dense stroma surrounding numerous slit-shaped epithelial profiles.
questions.stem: Which natural change would be expected with the patient's age?
options: The lesion may hyalinize and calcify in older women, producing popcorn calcifications
The lesion enlarges steadily after menopause and often transforms into a phyllodes tumor
The lesion regresses completely after menopause and does not hyalinize or calcify
The lesion enlarges to cause a bloody nipple discharge in later life
questions.explanation: Step 1. Compressed slitlike ducts in dense stroma are fibroadenoma. Step 2. In older women fibroadenoma may hyalinize and calcify, producing popcorn calcifications, and it is less prevalent after menopause.
choice_rationales: Hyalinization with popcorn calcification occurs in older women.
Fibroadenoma is less prevalent after menopause, and phyllodes tumor is a separate entity with leaflike stromal fronds, so it is not what a fibroadenoma becomes.
In older women a fibroadenoma may hyalinize and calcify, producing popcorn calcifications, rather than disappearing without a trace.

questions.condition_overview: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically in women under 35. It is a well-circumscribed, rubbery, freely mobile mass (breast mouse). Microscopically it combines proliferating duct-like epithelial structures with a loose cellular stroma, which can compress the glands into slit-like spaces. Growth is hormone responsive, so it may enlarge in pregnancy and regress after menopause. Risk of cancer is minimal, and management is observation or excision.

questions.case_context: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has bilateral breast enlargement. Biopsy shows scattered ducts in dense collagenous stroma with ductal hyperplasia and no acini.
questions.stem: What does the absence of acini tell the pathologist about the lesion?
options: It is gynecomastia, since the male breast has no lobules, and it does not raise cancer risk
It is a premalignant lesion that needs mastectomy because of its high cancer risk
It is a fibroadenoma, a benign tumor of intralobular stroma and glandular epithelium
It is lobular carcinoma in situ, with loosely cohesive cells expanding the acini
questions.explanation: Step 1. Ducts with hyperplasia in collagenous stroma and no acini are gynecomastia. Step 2. The male breast contains no lobules, estrogen excess in cirrhosis can drive gynecomastia, and gynecomastia is not considered a risk factor for carcinoma.
choice_rationales: Gynecomastia shows duct hyperplasia without lobules and is not a cancer risk.
Gynecomastia is not a precancerous lesion and does not call for mastectomy.
Fibroadenoma is a biphasic tumor from intralobular stroma, which men lack.
Lobular carcinoma in situ requires acini expanded by loosely cohesive cells, and acini are absent in men.
visual_clues: Several widely separated epithelial-lined ducts are embedded in abundant pink stroma.
questions.condition_overview: Gynecomastia is benign enlargement of male breast tissue from an increased estrogen to androgen ratio. Microscopically there is proliferation of ducts with a cellular stroma. Causes include puberty, aging, liver cirrhosis, obesity, drugs (spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, marijuana), Klinefelter syndrome, and hormone-secreting tumors. It presents as a subareolar, concentric, firm mass, unlike male breast cancer, which is eccentric and hard.

It is associated with a modest increase in cancer risk, so it is usually excised.

Breast size

Presence of a fibrocystic change
questions.explanation: Step 1. An irregular, angular lesion with projections is invasive breast carcinoma. Step 2. Stage with tumor size and axillary lymph node status is the key prognostic factor, with axillary nodal status the single most important, followed by grade and margin status.
choice_rationales: Axillary node status is the single most important prognostic factor.
Breast size is not a listed prognostic factor.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most common breast cancer (about 75 percent). It presents as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with stellate borders that may cause skin dimpling or nipple retraction. Cords, nests, and glands of atypical cells infiltrate a desmoplastic stroma. It is graded by tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic rate, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides therapy. It spreads to axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver, and brain.

options: Septate versus bicornuate uterus, distinguished by a continuous versus clefted outer fundal contour
Bicornuate versus didelphys uterus, distinguished by a continuous versus clefted outer fundal contour

questions.explanation: Step 1. Two side-by-side uterine structures behind the bladder indicate a duplication anomaly. Step 2. A septate uterus (nonresorption of the septum) keeps a continuous external fundal outline, whereas bicornuate or didelphys uteri (incomplete fusion) have an external cleft or separation.
choice_rationales: The fundal contour separates septate from bicornuate anomalies.
Bicornuate and didelphys uteri both result from incomplete fusion and both have an external cleft or separation, so contour separates them from a septate uterus, not from each other.

questions.condition_overview: A septate uterus is a congenital Müllerian anomaly in which the two ducts fuse normally but a median septum is not fully resorbed. The external uterine contour is smooth, with no fundal cleft, while the internal cavity is divided. The septum is poorly vascularized, so it is associated with miscarriage, malpresentation, and infertility. MRI or 3D ultrasound distinguishes it from a bicornuate uterus, and hysteroscopic septum resection corrects it.

questions.condition_overview: Serous carcinoma, particularly high-grade serous carcinoma, is the most common and deadly ovarian cancer and is thought to arise commonly from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fallopian tube fimbria. Papillary and solid sheets of markedly atypical cells invade stroma, with slitlike spaces and psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcifications). TP53 mutation gives an aberrant p53 pattern, and BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are associated. Patients present late with ascites and omental metastasis, and CA-125 is elevated. Treatment is surgery with platinum chemotherapy, and PARP inhibitor maintenance is used in BRCA or HRD-deficient cases.

questions.condition_overview: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant tumor of trophoblast with no villi, composed of sheets of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and intermediate trophoblast. It follows a hydatidiform mole, an abortion, or a normal pregnancy, or arises as a germ cell tumor of the testis or ovary. It forms a soft, dark, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass that invades the myometrium and vessels and spreads early to the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. hCG is markedly elevated. It is highly chemosensitive, and vaginal metastases should not be biopsied because they bleed.

questions.condition_overview: A complete hydatidiform mole is a diploid (usually 46,XX) androgenetic conception in which all chromosomes are paternal, so there is no fetal tissue. All chorionic villi are diffusely enlarged, edematous (hydropic), with a central cistern and circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia. The uterus is distended with grapelike vesicles, hCG is markedly elevated, and ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. p57 is negative because the maternal gene is absent. It is treated by suction curettage with hCG follow-up because 15 to 20 percent develop persistent gestational trophoblastic disease.

questions.condition_overview: A partial hydatidiform mole is usually triploid (69,XXY), from fertilization of one egg by two sperm, and an embryo or fetal parts are often present. It carries a much lower risk of persistent trophoblastic disease than a complete mole and is treated with curettage and hCG follow-up.

questions.condition_overview: Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) is the precursor of HPV-related endocervical adenocarcinoma. questions.condition_overview: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia) is the precursor of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma. questions.condition_overview: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) are benign papillary squamous proliferations caused mainly by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, spread by sexual contact. questions.condition_overview: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common congenital infection, acquired by transplacental transmission, usually after primary maternal infection. questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

questions.condition_overview: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma and the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, typically in young women. It forms a solid, pale, fleshy, lobulated mass. Microscopically large round cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. Cells are OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP positive. Tumors are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis. It can occur in gonadal dysgenesis, such as Swyer syndrome.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common breast cancer. questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

questions.condition_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a nodular proliferation of glands and stroma in the periurethral transition zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone and increasing with age. questions.condition_overview: Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation after 12 months of amenorrhea, at an average age of about 51, caused by depletion of ovarian follicles. Estradiol and inhibin B fall, so FSH (and later LH) rise, and the main estrogen becomes extragonadal estrone from adipose aromatization of androstenedione. Estrogen deficiency causes hot flashes, vaginal atrophy, sleep disturbance, bone loss and osteoporosis, and adverse lipid changes. Perimenopause is the preceding transition with irregular cycles, and treatment is symptomatic, including hormone therapy in selected patients.

options: A fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion, called Meigs syndrome
A benign teratoma component, called a dermoid
Peritoneal spread of ovarian cancer to the omentum, called an omental cake
Metastasis by lymphatics from stomach cancer, called Krukenberg tumor
choice_rationales: Meigs syndrome is associated with fibroma, a solid sex cord stromal tumor.
A dermoid is a mature teratoma with ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm tissues.
The omentum is a preferred metastatic site, and the mass is an omental cake.
Krukenberg tumors are solid ovarian metastases with signet-ring cells and are not an omental sheet.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A sheet of soft tissue replacing the anterior omentum in a woman with a complex ovarian mass is omental caking. Step 2. The omentum is one of the most preferred metastatic sites of epithelial ovarian cancer, so the finding indicates peritoneal spread and advanced disease.
visual_clues: The arrows follow a broad layer of abnormal tissue along the anterior abdomen.

questions.condition_overview: Epithelial ovarian cancer arises from the ovarian surface epithelium or fallopian tube and includes serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous types. It is often silent until advanced, with ascites and omental disease. Ultrasound shows complex solid and cystic masses with papillary projections, and CA-125 is often elevated. Staging is surgical, and treatment is cytoreductive surgery with platinum-based chemotherapy.
questions.case_context: A 61-year-old woman with a complex adnexal mass has CT showing a thick sheet of soft tissue along the anterior abdomen replacing the omentum, along with ascites.

The uterus, and through the lymphatics
The lung, and through the lymphatics
The ovarian surface, and by direct implantation

The uterus is not the typical primary named for signet-ring metastasis in the lecture.
The lecture does not name lung as the common primary.
Krukenberg tumors are metastatic and do not start on the ovarian surface.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Bilateral solid ovarian masses made of mucin-rich signet-ring cells are Krukenberg tumors. Step 2. The most common primary site is the stomach, and the tumors most likely spread to the ovary through the lymphatics.

questions.condition_overview: Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis to the ovary, usually bilateral, from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often of the stomach, and also the colon or breast. The ovaries are enlarged and nodular. Microscopically, signet-ring cells with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus infiltrate a cellular, reactive ovarian stroma, often with mucin pools. Prognosis is poor and depends on the primary site, and the finding of a bilateral solid ovarian mass should prompt a search for a gastrointestinal primary.
questions.case_context: A 44-year-old woman has bilateral solid ovarian masses. Biopsy shows mucin-rich cells with nuclei pushed to the edge of the cell. She has had weight loss and epigastric discomfort.

A dermoid cyst lined only by ectoderm, with malignant change most often to adenocarcinoma
An immature teratoma, which is the most common type and is usually cystic
A mature teratoma that is usually malignant, with transformation to squamous carcinoma in most patients

Mature teratomas are benign and make up 95 percent of teratomas, with only 1 to 3 percent undergoing malignant transformation.

Mature teratomas are benign and make up 95 percent of teratomas, but 1 to 3 percent undergo malignant transformation, most often squamous cell carcinoma, usually after menopause.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.
questions.case_context: A 23-year-old woman has a pelvic mass found incidentally. CT shows a cystic lesion with fat, calcification, and soft tissue. At surgery the cyst contains hair and teeth.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis, and what is the survival if it is confined to the testis?
options: Seminoma, with survival of 70 percent when confined to the testicle
Yolk sac tumor, with survival of 99 percent in adults
Teratoma, with survival below 50 percent
Seminoma, with about 99 percent survival when confined to the testicle
choice_rationales: The 70 percent figure applies to distant metastases, not to disease confined to the testis.
Yolk sac tumor is the most common testicular malignancy in males under 3 years.
Teratoma is not described here as having survival below 50 percent.
Seminoma confined to the testis has about 99 percent survival.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A well-defined homogeneous hypoechoic ovoid intratesticular mass in a young man is a seminoma, the most common cancer in males aged 15 to 35. Step 2. Survival is 99 percent when confined to the testicle, 96 percent with nodal spread, and over 70 percent with distant metastases.

questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Microscopically sheets or nests of uniform large cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and round central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes. Cells express OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP. It is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis, and it commonly arises in undescended testes.
questions.case_context: A 27-year-old man has a painless testicular swelling. Ultrasound shows a well-defined, ovoid, homogeneous hypoechoic mass within the testis. Tumor markers are mildly elevated.

questions.visual_target: Fibroid location across MRI examples
questions.stem: Which location is most likely to cause her abnormal bleeding, and what are the three names in order described?

The intramural fibroid, with the three being subserosal, submucosal, and intramural
None of them, since leiomyomas never cause bleeding
The submucosal fibroid abutting the cavity, with the three being intramural, submucosal, and subserosal
choice_rationales: The subserosal fibroid bulges outside the uterus and is farther from the cavity.
The order given in this option does not match the positions described.
Abnormal uterine bleeding is a common symptom of leiomyomas.
The submucosal fibroid is in contact with the endometrium and the order is intramural, submucosal, subserosal.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A mass in the wall is intramural, one projecting into the cavity is submucosal, and one bulging outward is subserosal. Step 2. Leiomyomas are the most common benign uterine tumor and commonly cause abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain, and the submucosal location is the one adjacent to the cavity.
visual_clues: Compare each mass with the bright cavity and the external uterine contour.

questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. They are classified as submucosal (beneath the endometrium, causing the most bleeding), intramural (within the wall), or subserosal (beneath the serosa, causing pressure effects). They are well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white-tan masses with interlacing bundles of uniform spindle cells without atypia. Symptoms include heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and infertility, and they shrink after menopause. Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is rare.
questions.case_context: A 45-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. Imaging shows three leiomyomas. One lies within the myometrium, one bulges into the endometrial cavity, and one bulges outside the uterus.
