Endometrial polyp in the first patient, and submucosal fibroid in the second patient
Cervical carcinoma in both patients, with extension into the uterine cavity
Endometrial cancer in the first patient, and hyperplasia in the second patient
choice_rationales: Distributed color flow fits a submucosal fibroid, and a single vessel fits a polyp.
The pattern is reversed in this option.
Cervical carcinoma is a cervical squamous cancer related to HPV.
Endometrial cancer and hyperplasia are discussed for thickening, not these Doppler patterns.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Vascularity spread through a cavitary mass fits a submucosal leiomyoma, whereas a single feeding vessel fits an endometrial polyp. Step 2. Leiomyomas originate from uterine smooth muscle cells and are the most common benign uterine tumor.
visual_clues: Look across the lesion rather than following just one isolated vessel.

questions.visual_target: Limit of endometrial morphology alone
questions.stem: Why can ultrasound alone not decide whether the thickening is benign or malignant?
options: Hyperplasia and cancer both thicken the endometrium, so imaging does not give the histologic diagnosis
Hyperplasia thickens the endometrium more than cancer does, so a markedly thickened lining on ultrasound reliably identifies the benign cause
Thickening excludes an endometrial source of bleeding in postmenopausal women
Cancer never thickens the endometrium on ultrasound, so any thickened lining is hyperplasia and needs no tissue sampling
choice_rationales: Both conditions thicken the endometrium, so imaging alone is nonspecific.
Both conditions thicken the endometrium and look alike on ultrasound, so thickness cannot separate them.
Thickening points toward an endometrial source and does not exclude it.
Endometrial cancer commonly thickens the endometrium, and tissue sampling is needed to tell the two apart.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickening can be due to hyperplasia or cancer. Step 2. Because both thicken the endometrium and look alike on ultrasound, tissue sampling is needed to establish the histologic diagnosis.

questions.condition_overview: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia) is the precursor of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma. It results from unopposed estrogen from obesity, anovulation, or estrogen therapy. Crowded glands with little intervening stroma are lined by cells with rounded, enlarged nuclei, loss of polarity, and nuclear stratification, which differ from the surrounding glands. A substantial fraction coexist with carcinoma, so treatment is progestin therapy or hysterectomy, based on the patient's wishes.
questions.case_context: A 63-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium. Another woman of the same age with similar bleeding also has a thickened endometrium on ultrasound.

questions.stem: What does the renal finding most likely indicate for the cervical cancer?
options: Local extension causing ureteric obstruction, which affects staging and treatment
A benign finding of the kidney that is unrelated to her cervical cancer
An adrenal metastasis that has spread through the blood from the cervix
Spread to the omentum through the peritoneal cavity from the cervical tumor
choice_rationales: Hydroureter and a dilated renal pelvis raise concern for ureteric obstruction by tumor.
The finding is a sign of obstruction in this setting and is not benign.
An adrenal metastasis would not explain a dilated ureter.
Omental spread is a feature of ovarian epithelial cancer.
questions.explanation: Step 1. HPV plays a role in most cervical cancers, and squamous cell carcinoma is the common type. Step 2. A dilated ureter and collecting system raises concern for obstruction by locally advanced tumor, and imaging is critical for staging, which determines treatment.
visual_clues: On the renal image, look at the branching central dark space and the adjacent tubular dilation.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cervical cancer and arises from persistently infected high-risk HPV lesions at the transformation zone through HSIL. Nests of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invade the cervical stroma. It presents with postcoital or abnormal bleeding, or may be found by screening. Staging uses tumor size, parametrial, pelvic wall, and nodal spread. Advanced disease can obstruct the ureters and cause hydronephrosis and renal failure, which is a major cause of death. Treatment is surgery for early disease and chemoradiation with brachytherapy for advanced disease.
questions.case_context: A 41-year-old woman with HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix has flank pain. Imaging shows a dilated ureter and dilated renal pelvis on the right.

questions.stem: Which zone is likely involved in each man, and why does the first man lack obstruction?

Peripheral zone in the first man and transition zone in the second, since the peripheral zone is away from the urethra
Anterior fibromuscular stroma in both, since it contains most glands
Transition zone in the first man and peripheral zone in the second, since the transition zone surrounds the urethra

Cancers arise mostly in the peripheral zone, and BPH arises in the transition zone around the urethra.
The anterior fibromuscular stroma is not the main glandular zone.
The zones are reversed in this option.

The transition zone surrounds the urethra and causes obstruction in BPH, while the peripheral zone lies away from the urethra.

questions.condition_overview: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which is the portion palpated on digital rectal examination as a hard nodule, and early disease is usually asymptomatic. BPH, in contrast, arises in the central and transition zone and causes obstructive urinary symptoms. Diagnosis is by core needle biopsy showing small crowded glands with prominent nucleoli and no basal cell layer.
questions.case_context: A 66-year-old man has an elevated PSA and no urinary obstruction. MRI shows a mass in the outer part of the gland, away from the urethra. His friend, age 72, has an enlarged prostate around the urethra with weak stream.

questions.tested_concept: Which injury and cause fit each man?
questions.visual_target: Stricture versus contrast extravasation
questions.stem: Which injury and cause fit each man?
options: Urethral tear from trauma in the first man, and stricture most often from gonorrhea in the second
Urethral stricture from trauma in the first man, and tear from gonorrhea in the second
Stricture in both men, caused by trauma to the urethra in both
Urethral diverticulum in the first man, and tear from trauma in the second
choice_rationales: Tears follow trauma with extravasation, and strictures are most commonly from GC infection.
The causes are reversed in this option.
Stricture is not due to trauma in the lecture example.
A diverticulum is an outpouching next to the urethra, not extravasation after trauma.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Contrast escaping the lumen after a straddle injury with meatal blood is a urethral tear, and a narrowing with contrast staying inside is a stricture. Step 2. Strictures are most commonly from gonococcal infection and are treated with antibiotics, balloon dilatation, or surgery, whereas tears are due to trauma and treatment depends on type and location.
visual_clues: Follow the white contrast column at each arrow.

questions.condition_overview: Urethral stricture is narrowing of the urethral lumen from scarring after trauma, infection, or catheter injury. A straddle injury can tear the bulbar urethra, causing perineal hematoma and blood at the meatus. Retrograde urethrography shows narrowing in a stricture and contrast extravasation outside the lumen in a tear, and treatment is dilation, urethrotomy, or surgical repair.
questions.case_context: A 30-year-old man falls astride a bicycle bar and has blood at the urethral meatus. A retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leaving the urethral outline. A different man with a history of gonorrhea has a narrowed urethral segment where contrast stays inside the lumen.

questions.visual_target: Periurethral outpouching across modalities
questions.stem: What is the diagnosis, and how is it usually treated?
options: Urethral diverticulum, treated by resection
Renal pelvic cyst, treated by observation with follow up imaging
Urethral stricture, treated by balloon dilatation only
Urethral tear from trauma, treated by antibiotics and catheter drainage

A renal pelvic collection would be at the kidney, not next to the urethra.
Strictures narrow the lumen and do not form a sac.
Tears are due to trauma and show extravasation.

questions.condition_overview: A urethral diverticulum is a localized outpouching of the urethral wall in women that communicates with the urethral lumen. It can cause dribbling after voiding, dyspareunia, recurrent urinary infection, and a tender anterior vaginal mass. MRI shows a fluid-filled sac adjacent to the urethra, and treatment is surgical excision.
questions.case_context: A 47-year-old woman has postvoid dribbling, pelvic pain, and recurrent urinary infection. Ultrasound and MRI show a small fluid-filled sac next to the urethra.

questions.tested_concept: Which developmental relationship explains the fetal fluid and also predisposes to the groin bulge?
questions.visual_target: Fetal processus vaginalis and scrotal fluid
questions.stem: Which developmental relationship explains the fetal fluid and also predisposes to the groin bulge?
options: A patent processus vaginalis keeps a channel open between the peritoneum and scrotum for fluid or bowel
Fluid infiltrating the testicular parenchyma from endometrial type tissue within the scrotum
Weakness of the abdominal musculature with age, producing a direct inguinal hernia
Reversal of testicular descent through the open channel, pulling the testis into the abdomen
choice_rationales: A patent processus vaginalis allows fluid or bowel to pass, explaining the hydrocele and the indirect hernia.
The fluid surrounds the testis rather than infiltrating it, and endometrial tissue is unrelated.
Direct hernias come from laxity of abdominal muscle over time, not from the processus vaginalis.
The testis is tethered by the gubernaculum and usually does not ascend, though the pathway stays open.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Dark fluid around, not inside, a descended testis is a hydrocele, and in the fetus a patent processus vaginalis gives continuity with peritoneal fluid. Step 2. The lecture ties indirect inguinal hernias to the same pathway, since the testis migrates and a patent processus vaginalis lets bowel herniate in. Indirect hernias are the most common type. The testis usually does not move back up because the gubernaculum tethers it.
visual_clues: Look for fluid around, rather than within, the fetal testes.
questions.ground_truth_confidence: high
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings and the associated teaching discussion on the cited pages.
questions.condition_overview: A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. In infants it results from a patent processus vaginalis that allows peritoneal fluid to enter the scrotum (communicating hydrocele). In adults it can follow trauma, infection, or tumor. It presents as a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates. Ultrasound shows an anechoic collection around a normal testis. Treatment is observation or surgical repair.
questions.case_context: A prenatal ultrasound at the end of pregnancy shows dark fluid surrounding descended fetal testes. A newborn boy from another family has a swelling in the scrotum and a bulge in the groin that appears when he cries. The teaching slide explains both findings from the same pathway.

questions.tested_concept: Which Doppler finding marks the active ovary, and what event can follow around day 14 because of this vascular state?
questions.visual_target: Perfusion comparison in resting and active ovaries
questions.stem: Which Doppler finding marks the active ovary, and what event can follow around day 14 because of this vascular state?
options: Increased low resistance flow, then follicle rupture that can send blood into the peritoneum or follicle
A high resistance waveform with reduced flow, and gradual shrinkage of the follicle without rupture
Absent flow to the follicle, and failure of the follicle to rupture at midcycle
Increased flow with a high resistance waveform, and persistence of the follicle as a scar
choice_rationales: Low resistance with high flow marks the dominant follicle, and rupture can bleed.
High resistance is the resting ovary's pattern, so it does not mark the active ovary.
Absent flow contradicts the markedly increased flow described for the dominant follicle.
The active ovary shifts toward low resistance, and the follicle ruptures instead of persisting as a scar.
questions.explanation: Step 1. The resting ovary has a high-resistance waveform, while the dominant follicle shifts to a low-resistance pattern with markedly increased flow. Step 2. That flow is among the highest in the body, and around day 14 the follicle is supposed to rupture. The lecture notes that blood can enter the peritoneal cavity, causing mid-cycle pain, or enter the follicle, which is a physiologic process.
visual_clues: Compare the Doppler signal and waveforms between the two panels.

questions.visual_target: Myometrial localization in the adenomyosis example
questions.stem: Which tissue relationship explains this woman's MRI, and how does it differ from her friend's condition?
options: Endometrial tissue grows into the uterine wall (adenomyosis), whereas her friend has extrauterine deposits and a homogeneous endometrioma
A smooth muscle tumor of the myometrium (fibroid), whereas her friend has endometrial tissue at sites throughout the abdomen
Endometrial tissue confined to the endometrium with a thickened junctional zone, whereas her friend has a uniformly homogeneous endometrioma
Endometrial tissue lining the ovarian surface (endometriosis), whereas her friend has adenomyosis in the myometrium
choice_rationales: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the uterine muscular wall.
Endometrial tissue in the junctional zone growing into the myometrium defines adenomyosis, and fibroids are muscle tumors that do not place endometrial tissue there.
Endometrium confined to its own layer would not alter the junctional zone, whereas tissue growing into the myometrium is adenomyosis.
Surface and abdominal deposits describe endometriosis, which is the friend's condition.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Endometrial tissue seen in the junctional zone and growing into the myometrium defines adenomyosis. Step 2. Endometriosis instead places endometrial tissue at sites throughout the abdomen, and an endometrioma appears uniformly homogeneous. The location in the uterine wall is why this patient has an enlarged, painful uterus.
visual_clues: Find the inner myometrium adjacent to the endometrial lining.

questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy.
questions.case_context: A 42-year-old woman has heavy, painful periods and a uniformly enlarged uterus. Pelvic MRI shows abnormality in the uterine wall centered on the junctional zone. Her friend has an ovarian cyst with homogeneous contents and endometrial-type tissue at several sites in the abdomen.

A has diffusely enlarged hydropic villi from a triploid conception with p57 positive staining, while B has two villous populations from a diploid conception with p57 negative staining

questions.condition_overview: Fibroadenoma (image A). Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically in women under 35. It is a well-circumscribed, rubbery, freely mobile mass (breast mouse). Microscopically it combines proliferating duct-like epithelial structures with a loose cellular stroma, which can compress the glands into slit-like spaces. Growth is hormone responsive, so it may enlarge in pregnancy and regress after menopause. Risk of cancer is minimal, and management is observation or excision. Phyllodes tumor (image B). Phyllodes tumor is a fibroepithelial breast tumor with a leaf-like architecture, in which a hypercellular stroma forms clefts lined by epithelium. It presents as a large, rapidly growing, mobile mass in women in their 40s to 50s. Tumors are graded benign, borderline, or malignant by stromal cellularity, atypia, mitoses, and margins. The stromal component drives recurrence and metastasis, so treatment is wide local excision.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) (image A). Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Immature teratoma is a malignant germ cell tumor of young women that contains immature, primitive tissue, most commonly neuroepithelium forming rosettes and tubules with crowded dark nuclei, along with mature elements such as cartilage and glands. questions.condition_name: Immature teratoma vs Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst)
questions.condition_overview: Immature teratoma (image A). Immature teratoma is a malignant germ cell tumor of young women that contains immature, primitive tissue, most commonly neuroepithelium forming rosettes and tubules with crowded dark nuclei, along with mature elements such as cartilage and glands. It forms a bulky solid mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Grade is determined by the amount of immature neuroepithelium, and it is treated with surgery and chemotherapy for higher grades. Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) (image B). Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

questions.condition_overview: Dysgerminoma (image A). Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma and the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, typically in young women. It forms a solid, pale, fleshy, lobulated mass. Microscopically large round cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. Cells are OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP positive. Tumors are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis. It can occur in gonadal dysgenesis, such as Swyer syndrome. Yolk sac tumor (image B). Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. Microscopically a loose reticular or lacelike pattern of cuboidal cells surrounds open spaces. Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space, and eosinophilic hyaline globules are common. Tumor cells secrete alpha-fetoprotein, which is a serum marker. It is chemosensitive.

questions.case_context: Two women have chronic pelvic symptoms. The first has heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. The second has dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility with an ovarian cyst filled with old blood. Tissue from the first is shown in A and from the second in B.
questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis (image A). Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy. Endometriosis (image B). Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

questions.condition_name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia vs Prostatic adenocarcinoma
questions.condition_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (image A). Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a nodular proliferation of glands and stroma in the periurethral transition zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone and increasing with age. Enlarged nodules compress the prostatic urethra, causing hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, and incomplete emptying, with risks of retention, infection, and bladder hypertrophy. Microscopically there are large glands with papillary infoldings with two cell layers, and basal cells are preserved. It does not become cancer. Treatment is with alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, or resection. Prostatic adenocarcinoma (image B). Prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common nonskin cancer in men and typically arises in the peripheral zone, so it presents late with urinary symptoms and is often found by PSA or digital rectal examination. Small crowded glands infiltrate between benign glands and stroma, lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli, and the basal cell layer is absent (p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin negative), while AMACR is often positive. Grading uses the Gleason system by glandular architecture: pattern 3 well-formed glands, pattern 4 fused or cribriform glands, and pattern 5 solid sheets, cords, or single cells with comedonecrosis. Bone metastases are typically osteoblastic.

questions.condition_overview: Ductal carcinoma in situ (image A). Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a malignant proliferation of ductal epithelial cells confined by the basement membrane. Patterns include comedo (high grade with central necrosis and calcifications), solid, cribriform, and papillary. It is usually detected as mammographic microcalcifications. Left untreated, a proportion progresses to invasive ductal carcinoma. Treatment is lumpectomy with radiation, or mastectomy, and endocrine therapy if ER positive. Lobular carcinoma in situ (image B). It is E-cadherin negative. It marks an increased risk of invasive carcinoma in either breast (about 8 to 10 times), so management is close surveillance or risk reduction.

questions.condition_name: Invasive ductal carcinoma vs Invasive lobular carcinoma
questions.condition_overview: Invasive ductal carcinoma (image A). Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most common breast cancer (about 75 percent). It presents as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with stellate borders that may cause skin dimpling or nipple retraction. Cords, nests, and glands of atypical cells infiltrate a desmoplastic stroma. It is graded by tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic rate, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides therapy. It spreads to axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver, and brain. Invasive lobular carcinoma (image B). Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common breast cancer. questions.condition_overview: Lichen sclerosus (image A). Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, probably autoimmune inflammatory skin disorder that mainly affects the vulva and perianal skin of postmenopausal women and also the penis (balanitis xerotica obliterans). Patients have intense itching and white, thin, parchment-like plaques that cause architectural change such as loss of labia minora and a narrowed introitus. It carries a small increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent or ulcerated areas are biopsied. First-line therapy is a potent topical corticosteroid. Squamous hyperplasia of the vulva (image B). Squamous hyperplasia (lichen simplex chronicus) is a benign thickening of vulvar epidermis from chronic rubbing and scratching, producing white, leathery plaques with acanthosis and hyperkeratosis without atypia. Intense pruritus is typical, and treatment involves high-potency topical corticosteroids and breaking the itch-scratch cycle. Biopsy of persistent lesions excludes lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma (image A). Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cervical cancer and arises from persistently infected high-risk HPV lesions at the transformation zone through HSIL. Nests of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invade the cervical stroma. It presents with postcoital or abnormal bleeding, or may be found by screening. Staging uses tumor size, parametrial, pelvic wall, and nodal spread. Advanced disease can obstruct the ureters and cause hydronephrosis and renal failure, which is a major cause of death. Treatment is surgery for early disease and chemoradiation with brachytherapy for advanced disease. Cervical adenocarcinoma (image B). Cervical adenocarcinoma arises from endocervical glandular cells, most often HPV-related (types 18 and 16). Irregular, crowded, complex malignant glands with atypical stratified nuclei invade the cervical stroma. It is harder to detect by Pap smear than squamous cancer because it arises high in the canal, and it can present with bleeding or a barrel-shaped cervix. Stage and depth of invasion guide treatment, which is surgery or chemoradiation.

questions.condition_overview: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) (image A). High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL, CIN 2 and CIN 3) is the true cervical precancer. It arises from persistent infection with high-risk HPV (types 16 and 18 most often), in which viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb. Immature basaloid cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, and mitoses occupy at least the lower two thirds up to the full thickness of the epithelium, with loss of maturation toward the surface. Diffuse strong p16 staining supports the diagnosis. HSIL is treated by excision or ablation because it can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) (image B). Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL, CIN 1) is a productive HPV infection of the cervical squamous epithelium. Atypical cells with koilocytic change are confined mainly to the lower third of the epithelium, and the upper layers mature normally. It most often reflects low- or high-risk HPV, usually regresses spontaneously, especially in young women, and is generally followed rather than treated aggressively. On Pap smear the finding is koilocytes with mildly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei in superficial and intermediate cells.

Papillary urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder cancer pattern and forms exophytic fronds with fibrovascular cores covered by urothelium. Low-grade tumors show orderly layering with mild nuclear atypia, while high-grade tumors show marked nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses, disordered polarity, and often necrosis. Smoking and certain chemicals are major risk factors, and patients have painless hematuria. Treatment is transurethral resection, with BCG for high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease. Urothelial carcinoma in situ (image B). Urothelial carcinoma in situ is a flat, high-grade noninvasive malignancy in which markedly atypical cells with large hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei replace the urothelium without papillae. It appears as red velvety patches, causes irritative symptoms, and cells are often shed into urine, so cytology is usually positive. It often progresses to muscle-invasive disease if untreated, and standard therapy is intravesical BCG.

questions.condition_overview: Malakoplakia (image A). Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory condition, most often of the bladder, caused by defective bacterial killing by macrophages, usually with Escherichia coli infection. Soft yellow-tan plaques form on the mucosa. Microscopically sheets of foamy, granular histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) contain round, targetoid, laminated, calcified Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. It is treated with antibiotics that penetrate macrophages. Cystitis cystica et glandularis (image B). Cystitis cystica and cystitis glandularis are benign reactive changes of the bladder caused by chronic irritation. Nests of urothelium (von Brunn nests) in the lamina propria develop central cystic spaces (cystica) or glandular differentiation (glandularis). They are common incidental findings and carry little malignant risk, although intestinal-type metaplasia may rarely be linked to adenocarcinoma.

questions.case_context: Two women have vaginal bleeding after pregnancy and markedly elevated hCG. Gross specimens from the first are shown in A and from the second in B.
questions.condition_overview: Complete hydatidiform mole (image A). A complete hydatidiform mole is a diploid (usually 46,XX) androgenetic conception in which all chromosomes are paternal, so there is no fetal tissue. All chorionic villi are diffusely enlarged, edematous (hydropic), with a central cistern and circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia. The uterus is distended with grapelike vesicles, hCG is markedly elevated, and ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. p57 is negative because the maternal gene is absent. It is treated by suction curettage with hCG follow-up because 15 to 20 percent develop persistent gestational trophoblastic disease. Choriocarcinoma (image B). Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant tumor of trophoblast with no villi, composed of sheets of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and intermediate trophoblast. It follows a hydatidiform mole, an abortion, or a normal pregnancy, or arises as a germ cell tumor of the testis or ovary. It forms a soft, dark, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass that invades the myometrium and vessels and spreads early to the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. hCG is markedly elevated. It is highly chemosensitive, and vaginal metastases should not be biopsied because they bleed.

questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyoma (image A). Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. They are classified as submucosal (beneath the endometrium, causing the most bleeding), intramural (within the wall), or subserosal (beneath the serosa, causing pressure effects). They are well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white-tan masses with interlacing bundles of uniform spindle cells without atypia. Symptoms include heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and infertility, and they shrink after menopause. Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is rare. Uterine leiomyosarcoma (image B). Uterine leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor that arises de novo rather than from a fibroid. It forms a soft, bulky, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass. Diagnosis requires marked cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and tumor cell necrosis. It spreads hematogenously, especially to the lung, and has a poor prognosis. It is treated by hysterectomy, and chemotherapy has limited benefit.

questions.case_context: Two women have malignant ovarian epithelial tumors. The first presents late with ascites, omental metastasis, and an elevated CA-125. The second has a mixed solid and cystic tumor. Sections from the first are shown in A and from the second in B.
questions.condition_name: Serous carcinoma of the ovary vs Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
questions.condition_overview: Serous carcinoma of the ovary (image A). Serous carcinoma, particularly high-grade serous carcinoma, is the most common and deadly ovarian cancer and is thought to arise commonly from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fallopian tube fimbria. Papillary and solid sheets of markedly atypical cells invade stroma, with slitlike spaces and psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcifications). TP53 mutation gives an aberrant p53 pattern, and BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are associated. Patients present late with ascites and omental metastasis, and CA-125 is elevated. Treatment is surgery with platinum chemotherapy, and PARP inhibitor maintenance is used in BRCA or HRD-deficient cases. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma (image B). Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is a malignant ovarian epithelial tumor with a mixed solid and cystic cut surface. Complex crowded glands and papillae are lined by atypical mucin-secreting cells and invade the stroma. Ovarian mucinous tumors are often metastatic from the gastrointestinal tract, so a bilateral or small tumor should prompt a search for a primary elsewhere. Treatment is surgery and chemotherapy.
